text: Abu Baker Asvat (/ɑsfat/) (23 February 1943 – 27 January 1989), also known as Abu Asvat or Abu, was a South African medical doctor who practised in Soweto during the 1970s and 1980s. Born in Fietas into a Gujarati Indian family, his father was a migrant shopkeeper, and he had two brothers. After attending local high school, Asvat studied medicine in Karachi, Pakistan, where he was involved in student politics, founded a student organisation affiliated with the Pan Africanist Congress of Azania (PAC), and hosted its cadres en route to China. He married Zorah in 1977 and had three children. Upon returning to South Africa, he worked at Johannesburg’s Coronation Hospital (now Rahima Moosa Mother and Child Hospital), but was fired after confronting a white pharmaceutical representative who refused to engage with black doctors. He took over a small surgery in Soweto from his brother, establishing a thriving practice that treated over 100 patients daily, often on a pro bono basis. During the 1976 Soweto Uprising, he treated children shot by police, and his surgery was protected by residents of a nearby squatter camp. He opened a creche and soup kitchen for informal settlement residents and was known as "the people's doctor" in Soweto. Asvat promoted the educational methods of Brazilian radical educator Paolo Freire and was drawn to the Black Consciousness movement, particularly Steve Biko’s concept of blackness. He served as a key link between Lenasia and Soweto, breaking racial and social taboos, and was beaten and threatened by a Special Branch policeman in 1978. He received the first annual human rights award from The Indicator, a Lenasia-based newspaper, where he advocated for social mingling and immediate action against apartheid injustices. Asvat was a keen cricketer and initially supported Ali Bacher’s "Normal Cricket" initiative allowing black teams to play at white grounds, but became disillusioned when racial segregation persisted. He co-founded the Transvaal Cricket Board (TCB), which rejected "multi-racial" approaches and instead promoted a "non-racial" vision, organizing successful boycotts and growing the TCB league under his leadership. He voluntarily stepped down as TCB leader in 1981 but remained active as a cricketer, playing for The Crescents and organizing a junior league in the late 1980s. In 1982, Azapo launched the Community Health Awareness Project (Chap), which involved Asvat and others travelling across South Africa on weekends with medically equipped caravans, treating between 150 and 500 patients and delivering health lectures to groups of up to 6,000 people. In 1984, he compiled a 20-page manual on basic healthcare, distributed in English, Sotho, Northern Sotho, and Zulu, and worked with the Black Allied Mining and Construction Workers Union to expose hazardous asbestos mining conditions. He and associates visited the Vaal Triangle in 1984 during unrest to treat victims and document injuries from apartheid security forces. By the mid-1980s, Asvat was frequently quoted in major newspapers and became a prominent voice in the anti-apartheid movement on health issues, criticizing the government’s handling of the emerging AIDS epidemic in 1988 and maintaining a regular health column in The Sowetan. In 1984, he hired Albertina Sisulu, a co-president of the United Democratic Front and wife of imprisoned ANC leader Walter Sisulu, as his nurse. Despite banning orders, Sisulu was employed, paid during detention, and allowed to visit her husband at Robben Island. Despite political differences between the UDF and Azapo, which led to violence, Sisulu and Asvat continued working together, treating casualties from both sides. Asvat advocated for Soweto squatters, rushing to assist those whose shacks were threatened by the Soweto Town Council and West Rand Administration Board, often arranging emergency shelter in Lenasia or feeding displaced persons in his home. He was elected president of the People’s Education Committee (PEC) in Lenasia, despite his Black Consciousness views differing from the pro-ANC stance of the group, which aimed to enable black youth education after the 1976 riots and campaigned for African children to attend segregated Indian schools, achieving success by 1990 when 15% of Lenasia students came from African areas. During the 1986 State of Emergency, unknown forces attempted to fire-bomb his home, and eight months later, he survived an attempted stabbing at his surgery, slightly wounded in the face, with Albertina Sisulu raising the alarm. His wife was routinely harassed by Special Branch police. In 1988, a gunman pulled a weapon on Asvat but fled when a patient entered the room. The authorities planned to develop the squatter camp where his practice was located in Soweto’s "Chicken Farm" area, but Asvat refused to move unless alternative accommodations were provided. He and Sisulu continued working despite power cuts, eventually relocating to Rockville, where they remained harassed by the Security Police. On 27 January 1989, two men arrived at Asvat’s surgery, claiming to need treatment; once admitted by Sisulu, they drew a firearm and shot him twice, killing him. Sisulu sat beside him as he died, later telling his relatives that "My son died in my hands." In the days before his death, Asvat became unusually fearful, drove home on a flat tyre and told his wife he believed an unspecified 'they' were trying to set him up, and made two attempts to see his lawyers the next morning. Investigations identified Zakhele Mbatha and Thulani Dlamini as suspects, who were sentenced to death for robbery (the sentences were commuted after the abolition of the death penalty), though no money was taken, and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) found the police negligent in assigning a robbery motive and failing to thoroughly investigate the attack. Rumours quickly emerged linking Asvat’s murder to Winnie Mandela, as they had first met during one of his rural clinics in Brandfort, where she was banished. Asvat provided medical care for her, and she regularly dined with the family and attended parties. After Asvat’s murder, Winnie Mandela claimed he was killed because he could corroborate baseless allegations that Methodist minister Paul Verryn had molested Stompie Seipei. Media reports circulated that Asvat had examined the boy and insisted he be taken to hospital, making his death part of a cover-up. In 2018, Fred Bridgland’s biography of Winnie Mandela argued she was behind the murder. The allegations stemmed from Kenny Kgase, one of four boys taken from Verryn’s manse and brought to Winnie Mandela’s Diepkloof house by her Mandela United Football Club, who escaped and reported seeing Stompie and being assaulted. Thabiso Mono, another boy, stated Winnie Mandela accused him and others of allowing Verryn to sleep with them and accused Stompie of being a police informant, and claimed he was beaten by Winnie and the United Football Club guards. Winnie ordered Katiza Cebekhulu to file a police report accusing Verryn, requiring a medical certificate from a doctor. Cebekhulu stated that Winnie shouted, “If you don’t cooperate, I’ll deal with you,” and left without Asvat providing the certificate, which angered her. Years later, Cebekhulu was ordered to show two youths, Mbatha and Dlamini, the location of Asvat’s clinic. At the TRC, Cebekhulu testified to a "volcanic row" between Mandela and Asvat after Asvat refused to support her false allegations. The hearings were adjourned due to claims of intimidation by Winnie Mandela. Mbatha and Dlamini testified that Winnie Mandela paid them R20,000 (equivalent to $8,000) and provided them with a gun to kill Asvat, and both claimed they were intimidated before testifying. Mbatha claimed he immediately implicated Mandela but was tortured into changing his statement to robbery. Dlamini’s 1989 confession implicated Winnie Mandela, but it was not presented to the court, with police justifying suppression by saying it was "at odds" with their investigation. Mbatha’s lawyers accused a group of men in combat fatigues linked to Winnie Mandela of intimidating his family during a TRC hearing. Winnie Mandela’s lawyer exposed inconsistencies in the testimonies. When Albertina Sisulu testified, she failed to confirm an appointment card placing Winnie Mandela at the surgery on the morning of the killing, claiming to have forgotten the details, and when questioned about not wanting to be remembered as having implicated a comrade, she denied it. Thabiso Mono stated he saw Winnie Mandela assaulting the boys with fists and sjamboks. During her own testimony, Madikizela-Mandela denied the allegations. The TRC’s final report stated it could not verify Winnie Mandela’s involvement, criticized the police for quickly concluding the motive was robbery and for failing to investigate the connection between Cebekhulu and Dlamini’s accounts, and deemed Mbatha and Dlamini’s testimonies not credible. In January 2018, prior to Winnie Mandela’s death, ANC MP Mandla Mandela, Nelson Mandela’s grandson by Evelyn Mase, called for a probe into Winnie Mandela’s role in the Asvat and Seipei murders. Asvat was buried the day after his death in accordance with Muslim rites at Avalon Cemetery. Thousands of people, both African and Indian, attended the funeral, with marchers toyi-toyied and singing struggle songs. Apartheid police attempting to seize Azapo banners were driven off by Lenasia residents, and many women were present. The section of the R554 road linking Soweto to Lenasia was renamed Abu Baker Asvat Drive by the post-apartheid government. A junior cricket tournament was instituted in his memory in 2002. In 2021, he was awarded the Order of Luthuli in Silver by President Cyril Ramaphosa.
